analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to pay double, not 1.5 times, the regular wage for overtime hours.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 2026 by five Democratic senators and referred to the Senate labor committee, where no vote has been scheduled; no Republican has signed on.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current federal law, workers who put in more than 40 hours a week must be paid at least time-and-a-half for the extra hours. This bill would raise that minimum to double pay, or twice the worker's regular rate. It would take effect 180 days after being signed into law. It would also raise the overtime floor in a few specific exemptions written into the existing law, such as certain provisions covering motor-carrier employees.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly and salaried workers who regularly work overtime hours. Anyone currently earning time-and-a-half for hours beyond 40 a week would see that rate rise to twice their regular pay, directly increasing take-home pay for the same hours worked.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers who put in overtime hours

how_it_helps.text: Rewrites the Fair Labor Standards Act so the overtime minimum is two times the regular rate instead of one-and-one-half times, for every place the lower rate appears in the statute.

Applies the same double-time standard to several specific overtime exemptions in existing law, including provisions covering certain transportation workers, so those carve-outs do not undercut the new rate.
Takes effect 180 days after enactment, giving employers about six months to adjust before the higher rate applies.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with overtime-heavy workforces — retail, restaurants, logistics, manufacturing, and healthcare operations — would pay roughly a third more for each overtime hour. Some may respond by scheduling fewer overtime hours, hiring additional workers, raising prices, or absorbing lower margins.

drawbacks.text: Employers facing a higher overtime rate may reduce the overtime hours they offer, so some workers could see fewer overtime opportunities even as the hours they do work pay more.

Small businesses and labor-intensive industries operating on thin margins would bear the largest cost increases relative to payroll, and some of that cost would likely be passed to consumers through prices.

The bill changes only the overtime multiplier; it does not raise the salary thresholds or redefine which workers count as exempt, so workers who are currently exempt from overtime rules altogether would see no benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who keep their overtime hours, the gain is direct and substantial — a third more pay per overtime hour. The main real cost falls on employers and, indirectly, on consumers through prices, and some workers may see overtime hours reduced as employers adjust scheduling. On balance the bill is a straightforward wage transfer from employers to overtime workers, with the usual trade-offs of a higher wage floor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in August 2026 and sent to the Senate committee that handles labor law; the committee has not taken it up, and no vote has been scheduled while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Senator Ruben Gallego introduced the bill on August 5, 2026, joined by four Democratic colleagues: Blumenthal, Markey, Merkley, and Van Hollen.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which is the standard first step for labor legislation.
No further action has been recorded since the referral — no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost on the merits: employers continue paying time-and-a-half, and overtime workers have not seen a raise. The practical beneficiary of the delay is the employer side, which avoids higher overtime costs the bill would impose.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, employers avoiding higher overtime costs

for.name: Sens. Blumenthal, Markey, Merkley, and Van Hollen

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on August 5, 2026 and has taken no action on it since — no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors are Democrats — 5 of 45 Senate Democrats — and no Republican has cosponsored; the committee it sits in is chaired by the Republican majority.

industries.industry: Employers with overtime-heavy workforces (retail, restaurants, logistics, manufacturing, healthcare staffing)
industries.note: The bill would raise the cost of every overtime hour from 1.5 times to 2 times the regular rate, a direct increase in labor costs for industries that rely on extended hours. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against the wage gain overtime workers would receive.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican-majority Senate and HELP Committee, no Republican cosponsors, and no committee action two months after introduction, the bill is very unlikely to receive a markup or floor vote before this Congress ends on January 3, 2027. Its realistic path is reintroduction in a future Congress or adoption of a similar provision in a larger labor package.
